articles.title_orig: Trump and Xi are set to meet in China amid tensions over AI. Here's what to know.
articles.title_zh: Trump and Xi are set to meet in China amid tensions over AI. Here's what to know.
articles.content_orig:
Washington — President Trump is holding a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, against the backdrop of a widening scandal over advanced U.S. chips reaching China and internal divisions within Mr. Trump's Cabinet about how to address it.
The bilateral meeting is taking place in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, known as APEC. Mr. Trump embraced Xi when he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday.
It's the third time the two world leaders are meeting face to face this year. The last time they met was in September, when Mr. Trump hosted Xi for a three-day summit at the White House. Mr. Trump is hosting Xi again for the G20 Leaders' Summit at Trump National Doral in Miami in December.
The Trump-Xi meeting will be followed by a meeting of Mr. Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Here's what Mr. Trump and Xi are likely to discuss.
Mr. Trump told reporters as he left for Asia that he may bring up Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The Justice Department has been investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed for diverting semiconductor chips to China.
The president has cast doubts on assessments that Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset.
"I don't know that she is a spy," he said. "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country, that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."
Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the scandal is much bigger than Jensen Huang and his alleged affairs.
"It's really kind of unfolded into a much bigger, longer-term scandal that involves the question of how many chips did China get, how porous were export controls, and how did the Commerce Department enforce them?" McGuire said on a phone briefing with reporters Wednesday. "Which I think is a much more important, longer-term strategic question for the United States, for the U.S.-China relationship than anything involving Jensen Huang's personal affairs."
Shortly before the president left for Asia, the Trump administration announced new interim trade rules that will restrict Chinese AI companies from accessing advanced U.S. chips remotely.
The move comes after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of slow-walking restrictions on Megaspeed, revealing a rift between Bessent and Lutnick. Bessent told CNBC that Mr. Trump had indicated that China should not have access to the chips, but suggested that Lutnick was resisting. The president didn't take sides in the Bessent-Lutnick debate, telling reporters before he left for Asia that the men have "two different views" where "one wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China."
"One view is you don't want to insult China," Mr. Trump said Monday. "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them. And the other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do. Both can say either is wrong or right."
Ultimately, the Treasury Department and National Security Council, not the Commerce Department under Lutnick, wrote  the new interim rule cutting off Chinese companies from remotely accessing the most advanced AI chips in data centers abroad, though the Commerce Department issued the rule.
"This is a very significant action that really cuts off a lot of the avenues that China is using to get AI computing power," McGuire said. "There was a digital forensic study that was done recently that showed that every single advanced Chinese model is actually trained with the most advanced American chips, so even though these chips have been banned to China, the controls have not been effective. They've probably had some impact but not that much."
The actions taken on Monday, however, will have a "really significant" effect on China's access to computing power, which "could materially widen the lead" between the U.S. and China on AI, McGuire said.
Mr. Trump has shown no signs of wanting to slow the United States' AI advancement in the race against China. After a September summit between Mr. Trump and Xi, the U.S. and Chinese governments pledged to set up a communication channel to share information when AI goes off the rails.
But talking about wayward AI incidents after the fact isn't nearly enough, said Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow on technology with the Asia Society Policy Institute and a digital fellow with the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI.
Graylin will be interested to see if Mr. Trump and Xi can work past the negative news cycle, like the Jensen Huang scandal, to take more steps on AI safety collaboration by bringing together more technical experts for working-level discussions.
"I hope that we go beyond just having surface level discussion, and we start to actually create some enduring institutions around safety," Graylin said.
Before leaving for Asia, Mr. Trump was asked if he'll bring up Taiwan in his meeting with Xi.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," the president responded. "I won't have to raise it."
David Sacks, a senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations — not the former White House AI czar David Sacks — said he thinks that's right.
"I think that it's very clear that every time Xi sees Trump, they do a little check-in on Taiwan, and Xi Jinping raises his concerns on Taiwan and his expectations of how President Trump will handle Taiwan and cross-strait dynamics," Sacks told reporters on the Council on Foreign Relations call.
A $14 billion arms package to Taiwan is still pending on the president's desk, Sacks said. Earlier this year, the Navy said the arms sale had been put on "pause" to make sure the U.S. military had enough munitions for the Iran war. Sacks said there will be "more pressure from Congress in the coming months to move that arms package forward."
"And so, if President Trump is determined to resist that, you know he will need, you know — Xi Jinping will hope to kind of stiffen his spine and say, 'You're on the right track, and if you approve this arms package, you're going to send cross-strait relations reeling.'"
Lyle Goldstein, the director of Defense Priorities Asia, told CBS News he is actually optimistic about a Trump-Putin-Xi meeting. Goldstein said he doesn't think any "major results" will come out of the sit-down, but the discussions might bear fruit in a future U.S.-China-Russia meeting.
"I actually think it could allow for some, not for breakthroughs, but for some movement on major issues," Goldstein said. "And this is the first time ever that you have this trilateral format for Russia, China, and the U.S. So I would like to see this continue."
Mr. Trump said he has a range of topics to discuss with both Xi and Putin when they meet, including denuclearization.
"We're going to talk about denuclearization," Mr. Trump said. "Tough subject, because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right? Especially since you do have other countries."
They'll also discuss Iran, the U.S. president said. On Tuesday, Mr. Trump said Iran would have a major price to pay if it detonates a so-called dirty bomb, after CNN reported U.S. intelligence indicates Iran may be developing plans to set off such a device in the nation's capital.
The White House previously said Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion in the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting, since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said Ukraine will be a topic for the three leaders.
"We'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine," he told reporters.

articles.title_orig: Dow slides 600 points, Nasdaq seesaws as Nvidia earnings bounce fizzles: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow slides 600 points, Nasdaq seesaws as Nvidia earnings bounce fizzles: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia shares sank around 2% Wednesday after the company issued its first earnings report since the departure of former CEO Jensen Huang .
Trading in the neocloud companies was volatile, as CoreWeave sank about 3%, Iren fell about 2% and Nebius whipsawed.
Nvidia's third-quarter revenue came in at $115.84 billion, more than $6 billion above analysts' expectations of $109.10 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion topped the $125.1 billion consensus, according to LSEG.
The semiconductor giant continues to navigate the fallout from Huang's resignation last week. Shortly before the results, Huang made his first public statement since resigning last week, saying that he was open to returning to the company, after an outpouring of support from prominent tech figures .
But Harvey Jones, the new and first-ever chair of Nvidia's board, said on the earnings call that the board does not intend to reinstate him as CEO.
″[Hyperscalers] are the ones that are right now feverishly looking for more focus in terms of the compute that we have available," interim CEO Colette Kress told Jim Cramer on CNBC's "Mad Money."
"This concept that anything is changing in terms of any of our types of customers — that is just not true. They are all continuing to be with us, and we have a very deep breath of different customers."
The U.S. Commerce Department announced a legal change on Monday to try and stem China's access to the most advanced Nvidia chips — which are already under export controls effectively preventing their import into the country — by restricting Chinese companies' ability to access compute remotely in overseas data centers.
In a letter Wednesday, the House Energy and Commerce Committee asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to appear to discuss chip export controls, and requested a briefing from interim CEO Colette Kress by Dec. 2.
Nvidia told investors in its earnings commentary that it was "not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China in our outlook," in keeping with its recent language on the country.
Huang is slated to appear before several Congressional committees in the coming weeks.
Speaking to CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Tuesday, Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., said Huang and Lutnick have agreed to appear before the committee in December. It's slated to be Huang's second appearance on Capitol Hill in December, after the former Nvidia CEO reached an agreement with three House committees to appear for closed-door interviews on Dec. 1.
— CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Stocks Fall as Nvidia’s Earnings Rally Sputters: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks Fall as Nvidia’s Earnings Rally Sputters: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) bulls are getting hit with another reality check in a saga now in its second week.
That is, with no visionary Jensen Huang at the company, Nvidia is, well, just another chip company — one that's searching for somebody to fill a giant black leather jacket in the C-suite.
Shares of the tech giant reversed sharply on Wednesday from an initial positive post-earnings reaction. Nvidia stock is down about 3.5% at the time of this writing, reversing an almost 4% premarket pop.
"We view recently ousted founding CEO Jensen Huang as a singular leader who leaves impossible shoes to fill. Huang's departure creates a leadership vacuum which nature (and investors) abhor(s)," Oppenheimer analyst Rich Schafer said.
Schafer said he still has no price target on Nvidia's stock given the volatility. He removed his price target several days earlier.
Interim CEO Colette Kress made a solid case late Tuesday for staying in the interim CEO role for perhaps longer than Wall Street expects. At the bare minimum, she made the case that Nvidia isn't being led by a group of rookies undeserving of being in the room with a Huang-level exec.
The company's third quarter was solid , the outlook strong, and Kress came across as a steady hand driving the Nvidia rocketship.
For the third quarter, Nvidia posted adjusted earnings of $2.68 a share on revenue of $115.8 billion. Wall Street had expected earnings of $2.47 a share on revenue of $109.15 billion.
Nvidia expects fourth quarter revenue of $127.4 billion to $132.6 billion, comfortably above the $125.25 billion analysts were looking for.
The company said it sees fiscal year 2028 revenue growth of 75%, up from a prior estimate of 70% offered just three months ago.
But pros tell us new Nvidia chair Harvey Jones — who joined Kress on the earnings call — botched the messaging around the timeline of selecting a Huang replacement. Jones lacked a sense of urgency on bringing in a permanent top-notch exec — not what a nervous market wanted to hear from a chip company at the epicenter of the AI boom.
"I don't know that any internal candidate, though, is capable of running the whole company," Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg said on Sozzi Unleashed . "Jensen famously built the structure of the company around himself. Like he's the center of the wheel and all the things connect to him. And I don't think anyone internally has as complete a view of the company as Jensen does."

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Gulf states and tankers under fire as U.S. and Iran ramp back up tit-for-tat strikes
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Gulf states and tankers under fire as U.S. and Iran ramp back up tit-for-tat strikes
articles.content_orig:
CAIRO — Iran widened its attacks on its Gulf neighbors on Wednesday, targeting a U.S. air base in Kuwait and launching several attacks on Bahrain in what appeared to be retaliation for American strikes the day before.
After about two months without such attacks, Iran has repeatedly targeted U.S. facilities in Bahrain in recent days. The small Persian Gulf island kingdom hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet.
The early morning attacks in the nearly nine-month-old war came after a U.S. fighter jet struck a Revolutionary Guard missile launch site Tuesday on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. strike was in retaliation for an Iranian attack on an American radar installation in Bahrain earlier Tuesday.
Iran said that its recent attacks — including those on other U.S. facilities in Bahrain on Sunday and Friday — were in response to U.S. drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers.
The tit-for-tat attacks come as the commander of the U.S. military’s Central Command, Adm. Brad Cooper, met Wednesday in Tel Aviv with Israel’s military chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, and the director of Israel’s intelligence agency Mossad, Roman Gofman.
They also complicate negotiations for a diplomatic solution and raise the risk of resumption of all-out conflict as a conflict in Yemen between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and a Saudi-led coalition could drag on for months.
The U.S. military didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest attacks.
With its economy suffering under a U.S. naval blockade and American military escorts helping restore the passage of oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz, experts say that the recent attacks suggest Tehran may be growing weary of the status quo.
“Even if neither side intends to enter a broader confrontation, the accumulation of military incidents across multiple fronts increases the risk of miscalculation and escalation beyond what either side originally intended,” Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group think tank, wrote in an analysis posted to X following the initial reports of the attack on Kuwait.
U.S. President Donald Trump has sent mixed messages on his next steps, saying new strikes are highly unlikely, but also sending a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops to the Middle East.
Though U.S. military protection has helped restore oil shipments from the Gulf, Iran has continued to attack tankers as they attempt to transit the Strait of Hormuz.
United Arab Emirates state-owned oil company ADNOC said Wednesday that one of its tanker crew members was missing after an attack in the strait on Tuesday, while 11 others were injured and were receiving medical care.
Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel’s military and intelligence services, described an “increasingly clear” pattern of attacks by Iran on shipping and U.S. facilities in the Gulf region.
“Iran appears to be pursuing a strategy of deliberate, calibrated escalation,” he wrote in an analysis on X. “The objective is not necessarily to trigger an all-out war, but to steadily increase the military, economic, and political costs of maintaining the blockade.”
He said that Washington is faced with the dilemma that a limited response may encourage Iran to push further, while a stronger response risks accelerating the escalation that the U.S. is trying to avoid.
“As long as the U.S. naval blockade remains in place and no agreement is reached, further escalation will become increasingly difficult to avoid,” he said. “There are two clear paths to de-escalation: a negotiated agreement or a U.S. decision to lift the blockade.”
After Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran on Feb. 28 to launch the war, Iran regularly fired on American facilities and interests in neighboring Gulf countries, as well as energy infrastructure and other targets.
In the attack early Wednesday on the Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait, the Iranian military fired at air defense systems and drone and missile launch platforms, according to a report on Iran’s state broadcaster.
Kuwait’s military said that its air defenses had intercepted drone attacks and didn’t immediately report any damage. The Kuwaiti Foreign Ministry condemned the repeated Iranian attacks as “criminal,” saying that they threatened the country’s security and stability.
During the war, Ali Al Salem Air Base has been struck at least 30 times by Iran, damaging or destroying at least 15 aircraft hangars, numerous warehouses and 10 buildings near a residential area, according to an analysis by The Associated Press.
The AP’s analysis used satellite imagery from multiple providers to help determine that Iran’s strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases in the Middle East focused on early-warning systems before hitting aircraft and buildings, causing billions of dollars in equipment damage.
AP also spoke to four regional officials who were briefed or had firsthand knowledge of what was hit. The AP found that, through August, more than 115 drone or missile strikes claimed by Iran or Iranian-backed militias damaged or destroyed structures on 26 military bases and other sites with U.S. equipment.
Under questioning before a U.S. Senate committee Tuesday about damage to the Navy’s regional headquarters in Bahrain, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said he couldn’t offer a full damage assessment in Bahrain because “it’s a nonpermissive area for us to go.” He told a reporter months ago that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain.”
Meanwhile, Bahrain’s Interior Ministry issued two alerts early Wednesday urging people to take shelter, followed by the “all clear” a short time later. The country’s military later said that it had intercepted a number of attacks from Iran, but gave no information on any damage or casualties.
Saudi officials have briefed allies that the conflict with the Houthis could last for another six months, according to a diplomat familiar with the matter.
The diplomat, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity, added that the kingdom in diplomatic talks is making the case that the military alliance working to restore the internationally recognized government in Yemen still must further set back the Houthis before it can begin credible talks with the rebel group.
The Iranian-backed Houthis control a significant swath of Yemen, including the capital of Sanaa, and have made territorial gains along the Red Sea coast in the current conflagration. They’ve also rattled the kingdom with missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi infrastructure, including on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and energy infrastructure.
The kingdom continues to make the case to allies that U.S. military support could help change the course of the war in the Saudi-led coalition’s favor, the diplomat said. But thus far, Trump has resisted the push from his ally for U.S. strikes on the Houthis.
Rising reported from Bangkok and Madhani reported from Washington.

articles.title_orig: DOT Secretary Sean Duffy keeps blaming L3Harris after FAA ground stop, even as cause remains unknown
articles.title_zh: DOT Secretary Sean Duffy keeps blaming L3Harris after FAA ground stop, even as cause remains unknown
articles.content_orig:
Transportation Sec. Sean Duffy said Tuesday that the previous week’s historic FAA ground stop was caused by a routine decommissioning of a router.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy urged a skeptical Congress on Tuesday to make a massive $50 billion investment in the nation’s air transportation system even as the Federal Aviation Administration took steps to prevent a repeat of last week's ground stop that caused chaos for travelers.
President Donald Trump has blamed old technology and Democrats for last week’s upheaval at the nation’s airports. But the FAA has been struggling to modernize the air traffic control system for decades — going back well before the first Trump administration. The agency said Tuesday it had paused installing routers linked to the ground stop.
Stream NBC4 newscasts for free right here, right now.
Duffy's request, which was detailed in a letter to lawmakers on Tuesday and cosigned by FAA chief Bryan Bedford and White House budget director Russell Vought, stated the money was needed “to deliver a truly world-class air traffic control network.” The $50.1 billion in funding would be divided into five distinct categories, each category getting about the same amount, including $10 billion for modernizing the air traffic control system.
“I hope they don’t piecemeal it. There’s been too much piecemeal happening over the course of 20 and 30 years. I hope we get the full investment,” Duffy told reporters before the meeting with Republican senators about the administration’s efforts to enhance air travel and safety.
The closed-door briefing was contentious, with the transportation secretary getting “yelled at” by multiple Republican senators, NBC News reports , citing to a person in the room who was not authorized to speak publicly about the private discussion.
Several Republican senators took issue with the request, and Democrats are even more skeptical . Lawmakers said they are for funding safety, but they voiced some concern about other aspects of the administration’s request, including billions for airport infrastructure and the replacement of aging terminals at key airports.
“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded. Some of that is not safety related,” said Sen. Ted Cruz, chairman of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science & Transportation, which has jurisdiction over air travel issues.
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., emerged from the meeting and told reporters, "I'm not going to vote for that."
“We’re not going to give them $50 billion,” said Kennedy. “But I think that we are willing to provide the money to replace the copper wires with fiber optics, and to try to stop the bleeding."
Another concern for Kennedy was the sudden increase of the funding request from $30 billion to $50 billion, calling the secretary's decision to use Friday's ground stop chaos as a reason to raise his demands "a huge mistake."
Another senator, Republican Rick Scott of Florida, said the airline industry should pay for many of the upgrades being sought, not the federal government.
Duffy did not meet with Democratic lawmakers on Tuesday. But, members in both parties noted that President Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” included $12.5 billion for air traffic control that still has not been fully used up. Pressed on the issue Tuesday, Duffy insisted that the $12.5 billion was insufficient for the specific upgrades he deemed necessary in this situation.
Still, some Democrats are vexed by the FAA's funding request amount.
“I generally support the idea of investing in air traffic control, but $50 billion sounds like an awfully round number,” said Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who’s poised to become majority whip and also sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee.
Duffy, meanwhile, said he’s open to other options that could include Congress breaking up the request into pieces, with the initial focus on the most critical needs for air safety.
As lawmakers debated the funding request, the Federal Aviation Administration took more immediate action.
FAA spokesperson Ian Gregor said the agency paused new installations of Juniper routers and disabled the functionality of all existing ones on Friday after technicians linked the problems to a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas.
The FAA said the Juniper routers linked to the ground stop serve as translators to allow the older analog part of the network to communicate with the newer digital parts of the network as upgrades are completed. So they serve a different role than the Wi-Fi routers that most people have at home.
The system became overloaded when the federal contractor that maintains the FAA’s telecommunications network was replacing outdated copper wires with fiber optic lines across the nation.
Duffy said the ground stop was needed after the installation of a new router by L3Harris in Arkansas resulted in a cascade of intermittent communications and radar signals at 17 of the 22 regional air traffic control centers. The centers direct planes cruising at high altitudes. A radar site in Amarillo, Texas, where a router had been installed three weeks earlier, also contributed to the trouble.
The FAA said that “excessive data” was flooding the system “at a rate of 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds.” That deluge created instability with “aircraft communications and radar feeds," the agency said.
For now, the FAA is relying on older Cisco routers that have been in place for 25 years to continue operating the network while they investigate the cause of Friday’s trouble.
The routers at issue last week are being tested in a lab at the headquarters of L3Harris.
Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper, said the company believes its “device functioned as it was configured by the installer” when the ground stop occurred. “The FAA is assessing the configuration and performance of all infrastructure involved to determine the cause,” the statement said.
Duffy said Tuesday that 68 previous installations involving the same routers worked well before this latest problem.
“We’ve been able to recreate what happened in El Dorado,” he said. “But the root cause of what happened, we don’t have clarity yet.”
Democrats in the Senate have called for halting the replacement of thousands of routers across the nation’s air traffic control system. They also demanded that the Trump administration provide clear answers about what went wrong.
“Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed. FAA must investigate further to determine the root cause and report to Congress on how it intends to prevent future issues,” said the letter sent to Duffy.
Equity research and brokerage firm Bernstein estimated the ground stop and the weekend work needed to recover from it cost the four biggest U.S. airlines $345 million combined.
The airlines had to offer cash refunds, credits or rebooking options to customers who decided to cancel their trips, Bernstein analysts said.
The lost revenue and additional costs from the ground stop still are enough to have a measurable effect on the quarterly earnings for American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines, the analysts wrote in a Monday research note.
“A booking slowdown before Thanksgiving, or a second outage, would cost more than the weekend’s cancellations did,” the analysts said, adding they did not see any signs of waning ticket demand.
Associated Press writer John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Israeli tanks roll into central Gaza in first ground operation since ceasefire began
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of displaced Palestinians fled their tents and shelters in central ‌Gaza on Wednesday as Israeli tanks advanced, in what the Israeli military said was an operation targeting Hamas infrastructure outside areas that Israel controls in ⁠the enclave.
Witnesses said some Israeli tanks rolled onto the main Salahudeen road, west of the Yellow Line that marks the boundary of the two-thirds of the Gaza Strip still under Israeli control despite ⁠a ceasefire that has ​lasted more ⁠than a year.
An Israeli airstrike near the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
The medics ⁠said separate Israeli airstrikes had killed two other people ​earlier ⁠in the day in ‌ Deir al-Balah and Gaza City.
An Israeli military spokesperson told NBC News that the military was carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of ‌the Yellow Line in central Gaza ‌and that it had struck a militant in southern Gaza earlier on Wednesday.
They later confirmed that it was the first ground operation since the U.S. brokered ceasefire came into effect in October 2025 .
Dozens of Palestinians, most of whom have been displaced multiple times since the start of the war in 2023, piled their belongings on top of bicycles, wheelchairs, motorcycles and vehicles as ​they fled the area.
Salam Aql said the military had ordered residents of the area to leave “but we wanted to stay because we ​are exhausted from being displaced so many times.”
“We are tired, I swear to God, we are tired. But as we were sitting there, gunfire started ‌coming ⁠in,” she said, adding that a boy was hit in the leg by a bullet.
“Once he was wounded, we could not stay any longer.”
Hamas said the Israeli military’s raid and forced displacement of Palestinians marked a ceasefire violation and a ​dangerous escalation.
The truce halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war, although it has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas’ disarmament.
The Israeli military spokesperson had no immediate comment on other strikes.
Residents reported hearing tank shells being fired in the area. An Israeli airstrike near the location of the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
Israel, which says Hamas has recently been regrouping and rearming, has stepped up attacks against the Islamist group. Hamas has accused Israel of attempting to derail the U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement.
Gaza health ‌authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been ​killed since the ceasefire went into effect, while ‌the Israeli military says five Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Palestinian authorities say more ⁠than 74,000 people in Gaza have been killed in the military campaign ‌that Israel ​launched there after Hamas-led fighters killed ‌about 1,200 people in southern ​Israel in an attack on October 7, 2023.
The body overseeing US President Donald Trump’s plan to end the Gaza war on Wednesday ​accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to meet their commitments to end hostilities, leaving the population of Gaza in dire conditions and the ‌ceasefire in danger of collapse.
The 12-page Board of Peace report, seen by Reuters, is the body’s second to the United Nations Security Council since the US-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a sobering assessment of progress made since then.
The board, established and headed by Trump, is expected to present the report’s findings to a meeting of the council in New York at ​the end of November.
“The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process,” ​the report said, warning that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely.”
While the ceasefire has halted major ⁠fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect ​last year.
Hamas agreed in July to a Board of Peace roadmap to surrender its weapons and transfer governance of Gaza to a civilian transitional authority, but Israel rejected the ​roadmap, saying it will not withdraw until Hamas is dismantled.
Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza, while the report said Hamas fighters have also continued attacks on Israeli troops.
“Every day that Israel continues strikes against Hamas targets, it delays putting Hamas’ agreement to the roadmap to the test,” the report said.
“Meanwhile, Hamas militant activity continues, the commitment to cease all military activities has not ​been met in full by the parties, and the population faces another winter in tents and rubble.”
Senior Hamas official Basem Naim dismissed the report as “pure disinformation”, accusing the ​Board of Peace of providing cover to Israel to evade its commitments under the plan to end the war and to continue its aggression in Gaza.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister ‌Benjamin Netanyahu ⁠and a spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.

articles.title_orig: Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China, where Xi Jinping’s family history runs deep
articles.title_zh: Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China, where Xi Jinping’s family history runs deep
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — It took a trip to China for me, an American, to see U.S. President Donald Trump in person for the first time.
Trump emerged from a group of black-clad photographers and other personnel surrounding him at a welcome banquet in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Leaders' Meeting held Nov. 17 to 19.
Seated just a few spots to his left was Russian President Vladimir Putin who picked up a glass of red wine to join a toast led by Chinese President Xi Jinping .
"At tomorrow's Leaders' Meeting, we will discuss measures to expand mutual opening up, explore pathways to innovation-driven growth, and identify opportunities to expand practical cooperation across various fields, so as to translate more initiatives into tangible results," Xi said in Mandarin, according to a CNBC translation.
Xi was speaking broadly, but Thursday's agenda includes a bilateral meeting with Trump, and their highly anticipated trilateral meeting with Putin.
But looking at the mood in the room, it seemed that their trilateral conversation had already started Wednesday night at their long banquet table. Much of what happens at APEC, including bilateral meetings and other exchanges between leaders, takes place away from the media.
But what struck me was how little sign there was of the tension surrounding Nvidia 's CEO Jensen Huang resignation, a controversy that has gripped markets for the past 10 days.
Ahead of Trump's entrance into the banquet hall, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao shared a friendly moment with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other members of the American delegation.
Last week, the U.S. officials said that Trump did not plan to raise allegations of Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy during his meeting with Xi.
It was a striking contrast to just two months ago, when I saw photographs of Huang and Tesla CEO Elon Musk sharing a table with Trump and Xi in Washington, D.C.
And when Trump visited Beijing in May, Huang took a few minutes to speak with reporters, including me, inside the Great Hall of the People. Musk was there too, accompanied by one of his sons.
This time, neither were visible in a room that was closely watched by the world. Musk was expected to join Trump's delegation in Shenzhen, but I did not see him Wednesday evening.
Their absence from the government-heavy banquet was striking. The world's most powerful leaders may be grappling with the implications of artificial intelligence, but they certainly didn't need the industry's biggest names at the table to do so.
China's Xi calls for removing trade and investment barriers
Putin says EU is losing industry, falling behind competition
Three things to watch as Trump, Xi and Putin meet in China
Over the months I've spent following APEC's "China Year," one thing has become clear: The forum has given Beijing an opportunity to host the U.S., Japan and other member economies at a time when unresolved tensions might otherwise have made such gatherings difficult.
But even in a year defined by talks of U.S.-China "strategic stability," the APEC events have exposed the rifts and the shifting dynamics in global power. Those dynamics were on display for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
Several hundred attendees, from Xiaomi CEO Lei Jun to U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue, arrived early for the opening of the APEC CEO Summit.
After waiting in silence for at least 10 minutes, the audience welcomed Xi in a distinctly modern way: by raising their smartphones to capture the moment. The applause was rather muted.
It was much the same at the more government-heavy welcome banquet that evening. So many attendees rushed to take their own photographs of Xi and other leaders entering the room that reporters' views were largely blocked.
Following Xi's morning speech, there was a lengthy intermission before Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim took the stage.
"The entire multilateral framework needs to change," he said, praising China on its "rare" recognition of smaller countries.
During the tea break that followed, attendees quickly resumed mingling. Some even brought coffee and snacks back into the room as Putin prepared to speak.
They listened as the Russian president talked about his country's economic resilience and claimed Europe was losing ground. As attendees headed to lunch, one thing stood out: Neither Trump nor any other G7 leader had taken the stage at the opening event. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke later in the afternoon.
The most visible American presence during the morning session came from business leaders appearing in a promotional video ahead of Xi's speech.
And the absence of an American voice was perhaps even more noticeable at Wednesday evening's banquet.
Trump did not follow Xi with a toast of his own. This was the same famously outspoken president, who in a winding speech in Davos, had declared that the U.S. must get Greenland .
Yet on Wednesday night in China, Trump wasn't the one holding the microphone.

articles.title_orig: 10-Year-Old NGINX HTTP/2 Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code on Servers
articles.title_zh: 10-Year-Old NGINX HTTP/2 Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code on Servers
articles.content_orig:
A flaw in NGINX 's HTTP/2 support can allow an attacker to run code on servers with HTTP/2 enabled, without needing to log in.
The decade-old flaw, CVE-2026-123007, dubbed " nginx2root ," has been present in NGINX's open-source code since version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015. Fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 came out today.
F5 , the company behind NGINX, says attackers can run code where ASLR is turned off or can be bypassed. Security researchers at Wiz said they bypassed ASLR and ran code through the flaw in tests. Xint's researchers said they ran code through it with nothing more than a reachable HTTP/2 port.
Code run this way gets the permissions of an NGINX worker process. Getting root on the host takes a second way to raise privileges, according to CIRCL, the Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg.
In Xint's tests, code running as a worker could get root on the host through a separate bug in the Linux kernel's SCTP code, even when NGINX ran inside a Docker container.
Neither the vendor nor the Wiz and Rapid7 researchers have reported any attacks exploiting the flaw so far. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog did not list it as of today.
Proof-of-concept code for the flaw is publicly available on GitHub, but its notes state it is suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started Docker container on the same machine.
Every open-source release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is vulnerable, according to NGINX's security advisories . That includes 1.31.8 from October 21, as well as the October 14 security releases 1.31.7 and 1.30.6.
NGINX Plus is affected too, in 37.x releases before the fixed builds and in R34 to R36, according to the vendor advisory .
Today's releases also fix four more flaws that the vendor says can lead to code execution under the same ASLR condition. It scores all five 9.2 out of 10 on CVSS 4.0.
Each flaw can be reached only in a particular setup:
HTTP/2 is on where a listen directive includes http2 , or where http2 on is set. Running openssl s_client with -alpn h2 against a server shows whether it accepts HTTP/2: the output reads ALPN protocol: h2 if it does. Behind a CDN, test the NGINX origin itself, because an origin that accepts only HTTP/1.1 cannot be attacked through HTTP/2.
These releases fix CVE-2026-123007, according to F5:
Versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 fix all five flaws, according to NGINX's release notes . On NGINX Plus, 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 fix four of the flaws, and the CVE-2026-123633 fix was introduced in the earlier builds 37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1.
After upgrading, restart NGINX fully or use its live binary upgrade. A reload alone leaves the old executable running, and existing connections can stay on old worker processes.
The official Docker images for NGINX had 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 tags as of today, including Alpine variants.
Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages as of today. Ubuntu's CVE status page listed nginx as vulnerable on its releases from 16.04 to 26.10, and Debian's security tracker listed it as vulnerable in bookworm, trixie, forky and sid. A distribution package can carry a fix without changing the version number that nginx -v reports, so compare the full package version with the distribution's own advisory.
The vendor lists workarounds for only two of the five flaws. For the resolver flaw, CVE-2026-123634, avoid SSI and mirror directives, and do not build a proxied server name from variables. For the mail proxy flaw, CVE-2026-113425, limit listeners to trusted networks.
CIRCL's response guidance lists turning off HTTP/2 as a temporary mitigation until you can upgrade. That blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, but not the other three flaws. Turning off HTTP/3 where it is used removes the setup that CVE-2026-121810 needs.
On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set http2 off; in each affected server block and remove http2 from its listen directives. On 1.9.5 through 1.25.0, remove http2 from the listen directive, so listen 443 ssl http2; becomes listen 443 ssl; . Then restart NGINX where needed and rerun the openssl check to confirm the server no longer accepts HTTP/2.
Until the Linux kernel's SCTP bug is fixed, the same guidance advises that hosts not using SCTP, a network transport protocol like TCP, block its kernel module from loading. One way is to add the line install sctp /bin/false to a .conf file in /etc/modprobe.d/ . That does not unload a module already loaded or turn off SCTP built into the kernel.
For signs of an attack, CIRCL suggests looking for NGINX workers that start unexpected programs, workers that exit abnormally or leave core dumps, long-lived HTTP/2 connections with heavy incoming traffic but few logged requests, and unusual outbound connections or DNS lookups. A clean access log does not rule out an attack, because HTTP/2 control frames do not normally show up there as requests. None of these signs is proof on its own.
Rapid7's version of the attack needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, according to its technical analysis . The attack took two and a half minutes in its demonstration. On links slower than about 300 Mbit/s, the transfer would run past NGINX's default one-hour connection limit, and the attack would fail.
The method also depends on a glibc memory-copy routine that is chosen on x86-64 CPUs with the avx512f and avx512vl features.
Wiz ran its tests on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds, using HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems, according to its disclosure post .
Xint's attack worked against its test servers on AWS, GCP and Azure, including over a public IP address, according to its research report .

articles.title_orig: Americans will pay more for Thanksgiving dinners this year, Farm Bureau says
articles.title_zh: Americans will pay more for Thanksgiving dinners this year, Farm Bureau says
articles.content_orig:
For the first time since 2022, American shoppers will see an increase in the price of goods for Thanksgiving dinner. Results from the American Farm Bureau Federation's 41st annual Thanksgiving dinner cost survey indicate that the price of a Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people averages $58.63, up 6% from a year ago.
Over Four Decades of AFBF Thanksgiving Surveys
Each November, as millions of Americans prepare to gather with their family and friends to celebrate Thanksgiving, hundreds of volunteer shoppers from all 50 states and Puerto Rico participate in AFBF's annual Thanksgiving dinner cost survey. Every year since 1986, shoppers have reported prices for a standard list of items at their local grocery store for a variety of ingredients used to craft Thanksgiving favorites. Up until 2018, the survey included carrots, celery, cranberries, cubed stuffing, dinner rolls, frozen green peas, sweet potatoes, pumpkin pie mix, frozen pie crusts, whole milk, heavy whipping cream, and the ubiquitous American holiday staple: turkey. In 2018, AFBF added ham, frozen green beans and russet potatoes to better reflect the price of an all-American Thanksgiving meal.
While the overall cost of Thanksgiving dinner ticked upward in 2026, prices for several items included in the survey decreased slightly from 2025. A vegetable tray containing celery and carrots posted the largest percentage decline in this year's survey, with a 3.7% decrease compared to a year ago. In terms of absolute dollar changes, frozen pie crusts had the sharpest decrease, posting a decrease of 9 cents compared to a year ago. The survey bodes well for pumpkin pie enthusiasts, who will enjoy a lower overall cost for their beloved dessert despite an increase in the cost of pumpkin pie mix, as heavy whipping cream is also cheaper in 2026 compared to last year.
Higher Prices for Several Thanksgiving Favorites
The overall cost of a 10-person Thanksgiving dinner increased for 2026, largely fueled by increases in items key to the Turkey Day menu. The most notable increase for 2026 is the turkey itself, with the average price of a 16 pound frozen bird being $23.68, an increase of $2.38 (10%) from 2025. As discussed in a recent Farm Bureau Intel , strong demand and tight inventories have led to increased prices for turkey in 2026.
Apart from turkey, other widely featured Thanksgiving items increased in this year's survey. Grocery store prices for boneless ham, milk, dinner rolls, sweet potatoes, russet potatoes, frozen peas, frozen green beans, cranberries, and cubed stuffing (known in some regions as “dressing”) all increased in 2026.
Higher prices for these items aren't a complete surprise, as the effects of significant spikes in prices for critical inputs throughout the supply chain, like fuel for processing and transportation, have made their way to consumers. America's farmers and ranchers also face significant challenges, with record diesel costs, elevated fertilizer prices, increased labor expenses, and a bigger bill for items like rent and electricity — all of which hurt their ability to breakeven at the end of the year. However, unlike wholesalers and retailers, farmers aren’t able to pass those costs up the supply chain
Thanksgiving Dinner Prices Vary Across the Country
At an average of $61.57 for a 10-person classic Thanksgiving dinner, the Northeast has the highest cost. The Northeast's dinner basket cost is about 5% higher than the national average.  The average cost for a Thanksgiving dinner for 10 in the West and Midwest is closer to the national average, at $58.74 and $56.89, respectively. The South's average dinner cost is $54.33.
Some Shoppers May Find Great Deals
Despite the overall increase in the average cost of Thanksgiving dinner this year, some of our shoppers were able to find staggering deals on a variety of items, including turkey, which some shoppers reported finding  for as low as 69 cents per pound, nearly half the average nationwide price for a pound of turkey.  As Thanksgiving approaches, shoppers will look for deals on a variety of items to bring down the cost of their Thanksgiving dinner grocery list.
Higher Grocery Prices Do Not Mean Higher Farm Profits
Farm Bureau's 2026 Thanksgiving Dinner market basket survey indicates that Americans will pay more to feed family and friends this Thanksgiving. Nearly all items surveyed increased in price compared to 2025, with turkey, milk and cranberries posting some of the largest year-over-year percentage gains. However, higher grocery prices do not necessarily translate into better returns for America's farmers and ranchers.
Farmers and ranchers are largely price-takers, not price-makers, and receive only a small share of what consumers spend at the grocery store. USDA's Food Dollar Series estimates that less than 6 cents of every dollar spent on food goes back to the farm. Even when higher retail prices translate into increased farm revenue, rising production costs can quickly offset those gains. Elevated prices for critical inputs such as diesel, fertilizer and equipment continue to squeeze farm margins.
For example, this year's survey found that a 12-ounce bag of cranberries costs nearly 9% more than last year. That increase does not necessarily mean the Wisconsin cranberry farmer who grew them is receiving a higher price. Even if the farmer does capture some additional revenue, those earnings are needed to cover increased fertilizer, fuel and other production expenses.
As Americans gather around the Thanksgiving table, it's important to remember that higher food prices can place pressure on both consumers and the farmers who produce that food. Wherever and however you celebrate this Thanksgiving, take a moment to thank America's farmers and ranchers, who continue working through challenging economic conditions to provide the food, fuel and fiber we rely on every day.

articles.title_orig: Trump is trying to put the Iran war behind him, but it’s not over
articles.title_zh: Trump is trying to put the Iran war behind him, but it’s not over
articles.content_orig:
Trump against the backdrop of the Strait of Hormuz | Photo: CENTCOM, Reuters, AFP
With the US midterm elections over, President Donald Trump faces a dilemma over how to bring the war with Iran to an end.
The president's advisers have presented three options. The first, championed by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, calls for targeted strikes against nuclear and ballistic missile facilities rebuilt since the ceasefire, as well as regime targets, including bases belonging to the Basij militia and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, along with civilian infrastructure and oil facilities. The goal is to weaken the regime in the hope that it will collapse.
The second option is a deal with Iran, an effort led by Vice President JD Vance and Steve Witkoff. At this stage, however, Trump's frustration with Iran's intransigence appears to have exhausted his patience for negotiations. He has therefore sent Vance to deal with the fallout from the midterm elections.
The third option is to maintain the blockade of Iranian ports and continue strangling the country's collapsing economy, an approach led by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
The blockade of Iranian ports and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping and oil tankers have so far proved successful. A report by the International Energy Agency (IEA) indicates that the oil market is moving into surplus in the final quarter of 2026, while inventories are beginning to recover. Oil prices are gradually declining and have fallen below $100 a barrel.
There is no doubt that the US operation to reopen the strait has succeeded, dealing a severe blow to the Iranians, who have lost the last strategic weapon at their disposal. Iran's economy is collapsing, and the murderous regime of the ayatollahs is struggling to govern the country and provide its people with basic necessities.
Iran's rulers understand that, under the current strategic circumstances, only the possession of nuclear weapons can ensure their survival. They believe a nuclear deterrent would enable them to bring an end to the blockade and sanctions and begin rebuilding the country.
The Trump administration, for its part, understands Iran's motivations. Following his party's defeat in the midterm elections, Trump himself wants to go down in history as the president who prevented Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and succeeded in toppling its reign of terror.
On the ground, US forces are making considerable efforts to keep the strait open, exposing Navy vessels to attacks by Iranian unmanned aerial vehicles and drones. The operation requires a sustained American military presence in and around the strait, both at sea and in the air.
In this type of conflict, the Iranians employ terrorist tactics that complicate US operations. It is a form of ongoing security warfare that the IDF knows well from its various theaters of operation, requiring substantial manpower and the adaptation of tactics and equipment to changing conditions. Such an operation demands sustained American resolve.
The arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt brings the number of US aircraft carriers in the region to three, providing sufficient military power to launch significant strikes across Iran. It seems unlikely that a force of this size will remain in the region for long. At some point, the USS George Washington is expected to return to Japan.
USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) sails with USS George Washington (CVN 73) in the Arabian Sea, Nov. 17. https://t.co/KCP22Iikx1
â U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) November 17, 2026
Trump will spend the coming week in Southeast Asia, where he is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, before returning to the US toward the end of the week. His return is expected to open a window of roughly two weeks for a possible strike.
Israel would be an integral part of any attack, should one take place, and would even lead some of the strikes.
IDF soldiers and commanders should be sent into battle by a united government capable of leading the country. Israel's complicated political situation will require party leaders to make difficult decisions. A war against Iran, which would likely also involve Hezbollah, should be conducted under the leadership of a national unity government.

articles.title_orig: Russell Brand faces prison transfer after ‘appalling’ YouTube message
articles.title_zh: Russell Brand faces prison transfer after ‘appalling’ YouTube message
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The government has asked Google to deactivate Russell Brand’s YouTube account after it was used to issue an “appalling” message from his cell protesting his innocence , according to a report.
A source told Sky News that a justice minister had met with representatives from the company to make the request.
It follows the suspension of Brand's profiles on Instagram and Facebook by parent company Meta after he was found guilty of rape and sexual assault.
The Independent has contacted Google and the Ministry of Justice for comment.
Following the incident, prison officials are understood to have decided to move Brand to another jail, sources told The Times .
It is unknown where Brand will be transferred to, but he had previously been assessed for HMP Wakefield , which is home to some of Britain’s most notorious serial killers, murderers and rapists.
However, the prison, where disgraced Lostprophets singer Ian Watkins was stabbed to death, was deemed to be too dangerous for Brand, the publication said.
Brand was jailed for 10-and-a-half years earlier this month for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.
In a statement shared on YouTube by his wife, Laura Gallacher, on Sunday, the former Hollywood star claimed: “I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for.”
A Downing Street spokesman condemned the “appalling” message and said the matter was being urgently investigated because prisoners are strictly prohibited from making statements that cause distress to victims.
Brand was already transferred to the lower-security Category C prison, HMP Littlehey, on Friday from HMP Wandsworth.
His move was first reported by The Sun , which said concerns for Brand’s safety and him being deemed a low escape risk could have prompted his transfer. The prison is for men who cannot be trusted in an open prison but are judged unlikely to try to abscond.
A prison source told the newspaper that Brand’s calls will now be listened to by staff and that the rapist will face far greater scrutiny if he is moved to a higher-security prison.
Investigators will reportedly determine whether Brand’s message was an attempt to influence accusers whose allegations are currently being investigated by police.
Brand’s message said: “Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support.
“As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.
“The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do.
“I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey, little as in small, and hey as in hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe.
“The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated.
“And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone.”
He added: “I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me. Let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us.”
Former prison governor John Podmore told the BBC: “We cannot stop him speaking to his wife. We cannot stop his wife relaying his thoughts, his views and his comments.
"Those views are normally being conveyed to his followers on his channel and we can’t do anything about that.
“But I’ve been listening to TV and radio in the past 24 hours and most other people have done that, and it’s enormously disrespectful for the victims.
“So yes, let’s have a look at the rules. Let’s have rules that pertain to the way social media works, but the prison service lives in an analogue age and it’s not about to change any time soon, I’m afraid. But if the government wants to do something, [it] should do it.”
The prime minister’s spokesman added: “Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims. And speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances. Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments.”
Brand is now facing a string of fresh sexual assault and rape allegations, including one made by a 16-year-old schoolgirl.
Under the sentence he received on Monday, he is expected to serve two-thirds of his prison sentence before being released on licence.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia interim CEO says 'we’ve got this' as company looks to future without Jensen Huang
articles.title_zh: Nvidia interim CEO says 'we’ve got this' as company looks to future without Jensen Huang
articles.content_orig:
Humilis Investment Strategies CEO and CIO Brian Belski joins Taylor Riggs to analyze Nvidia's third-quarter earnings beat, showing a 103% year-over-year revenue surge. They also discuss the board's decision regarding Jensen Huang.
Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday's earnings call that the company is well-positioned to move forward following the abrupt resignation of co-founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang last week following the revelation of extramarital affairs.
Kress, who has served as Nvidia's CFO since 2013, delivered the AI giant's first quarterly earnings report since Huang's departure, which beat the market's expectations in terms of revenue and earnings per share.
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We've got this," Kress said on the call.
"With the market-leading multiyear roadmap, supply agreements extending through to the end of the decade and sustainable demand, we are well positioned to accelerate Nvidia's leadership position," she added.
NVIDIA RELEASES QUARTERLY EARNINGS, SUGGESTS FUTURE PLANS AFTER JENSEN HUANG'S RESIGNATION
Nvidia's quarterly earnings beat the market's expectations in its first report since Jensen Huang's resignation. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Investors were looking for the company to provide reassurance about its path forward as well as to post strong results over the prior three months in what was viewed as a test for the durability of the AI trade .
Nvidia's earnings beat analysts' estimates for quarterly revenue , which came in at $115.8 billion and topped the estimate of $109.1 billion reflected in data compiled by LSEG. Diluted earnings per share were $2.68, beating the estimate of $2.48.
Revenue was up 20% on a quarterly basis and 103% year over year, while earnings per share rose 10% from the prior quarter and 108% from a year ago. Nvidia's net income for the quarter was $65.3 billion, which represents a quarterly increase of 9% and a rise of 105% year over year.
Nvidia lifted its forecast for the fourth quarter of its fiscal 2027, which includes an additional week, to project $130 billion in revenue, plus or minus 3%; while Kress said the company raised its fiscal year 2028 outlook with revenue growth of 75% year over year, an increase from 70%.
JENSEN HUANG SAYS HE IS WILLING TO RETURN AS NVIDIA CEO, SAYING 'I OWN MY MISTAKES COMPLETELY'
Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO. (Nvidia/Handout)
She also noted that Nvidia's cloud industry backlog grew to $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago, which underscored the "significant multiyear opportunity ahead of our partners and of Nvidia."
Earlier on Tuesday before the earnings release, Huang released a statement saying that "I own my mistakes completely" and that he would be open to returning as the company's CEO if the board of directors thought it would be "in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America."
Harvey Jones, chairman of the Nvidia board of directors, shut down that speculation on the earnings call, saying that Huang voluntarily resigned and the board "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO."
NVIDIA ADDS BOARD OVERSIGHT OF NATIONAL SECURITY AND EXPORT COMPLIANCE
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would be willing to return as CEO after resigning last week, though the board chairman later said directors don't plan to do so. (Soeren Stache/picture alliance via Getty Images)
The chairman said that the company will consider internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent CEO. He added that while the board would like to name the permanent CEO soon, it isn't in a rush to do so and "won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person."
Jones also praised Kress, saying that "Colette has been at the center of this company's extraordinary growth for the last 13 years, instrumental in executing strategy and with a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position."

Nvidia shares were down about 2% in late morning trade on Wednesday following the release of the quarterly earnings report after the closing bell on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.content_orig:
Bill Ackman had some strong words for Nvidia's board of directors following the chip giant's earnings report on Tuesday.
The billionaire founder of Pershing Square Capital Management  said the board was not acting in the best interests of investors by resisting calls to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang.
Huang's sudden resignation from Nvidia over after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, has divided the investing community. The company said on Tuesday's earnings call that the board has no plans to bring him back.
"I believe the @nvidia board is not acting in the best interest of shareholders nor in a manner consistent with their fiduciary duties," Ackman wrote in an X post on Wednesday.
This isn't the first time that Ackman has advocated for Huang to be reinstated. At a recent conference, he outlined a path for the AI stalwart to bring back its former top executive, though he noted that it would hinge on Huang being cleared of any activity related to national security risks.
While investigations into Huang's alleged involvement with Chinese tech executive Alice Huang remain ongoing, others seem to share Ackman's sentiment that the former CEO should get his job back.
A petition urging Nvidia's board to reinstate him has garnered over 108,000 signatures, including Elon Musk. The campaign's website claims that over 58,000 shareholders and 5,600 company staff members have signed it.
Ackman hasn't confirmed if he's one of the signees of the petition, but he said he has problems with how the board handled Huang's departure.
"They did so without careful consideration of the impact on the company, its customers, its shareholders or other stakeholders," he said. "They rushed to judgment without the benefit of careful due diligence or even with a basic understanding of the facts."
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
The hedge fund manager added that he based his view on how quickly Huang stepped down following the scandal breaking and how little information the company provided at the time his resignation was announced.
In Ackman's opinion, the time allowed for one virtual board meeting at the most, something that he noted often takes time to assemble. The fund manager expressed strong skepticism that the board had enough time to properly assess the facts and decide how to handle what ultimately became Huang's resignation.
"And now the board is compounding its failures by insisting that there is no possibility for Jensen's return as CEO," Ackman said. "The board's conduct here is shocking for a company of this scale and importance to our country and the world at large, particularly at this moment in history."
Nvidia's board of did not respond to a request for comment on Ackman's statements.

articles.title_orig: The Fed's next moves come into focus
articles.title_zh: The Fed's next moves come into focus
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Federal Reserve governor Chris Waller said Wednesday that if the central bank hikes interest rates by a quarter point next month, it will need to signal that the Fed will hike again by that much in January.
Otherwise, the Fed needs to raise rates by a jumbo half percentage point in December.
"People have argued, do you do 50 in December, nothing in January, or 25 in December, 25 in January," Waller said in an interview Wednesday on CNBC. "But when you do 25 now and you're going to do 25 in January, it only affects market pricing if you signal you're going to do it, and you give the markets a credible signal."
Waller said that if you leave the market guessing about a January rate increase, there won't be an effect on the market and, by extension, the economy.
"If you're not going to signal this very clearly to markets you're going in January, my view is then you have to go 50 in December," Waller said.
Read more: How the Fed rate decision affects your bank accounts, loans, credit cards, and investments
That sounds a lot like forward guidance, which Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has sought to eliminate since taking the reins in May. Warsh has said that telegraphing future policy moves distorts market signals and boxes in policymakers.
But Warsh's philosophy hasn't quite taken hold, as other Fed members have continued to offer clues about the path ahead — which has also led to more questions and at times confusion in markets.
Without using the term explicitly, Waller argued Wednesday that the Fed would need to use forward guidance if it doesn't deliver a jumbo hike next month. He said the central bank could signal its next move either in the statement or at Warsh's press conference. He added that quarterly interest rate projections, which will be released in December, would be helpful this time because it's the end of the year and the projections would be for all of next year.
Waller said the Fed needs to be more aggressive because inflation is moving higher after remaining above the central bank's 2% goal for nearly six years.
Read more: How to protect your savings against inflation
Waller first hinted at a jumbo hike last week, saying ahead of the Consumer Price Index release, that if inflation came in higher than expected, stronger action would be needed.
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October, compared with expectations of 0.3%. "Core" inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3%, compared with expectations of 0.2%.
On Wednesday, Waller said the Fed needs to take back the three rate cuts from last year and may need to do more to get inflation to come back down.
New York Federal Reserve president John Williams doesn't share that view.
Asked Tuesday during a Q&A with Axios in New York whether that latest inflation data calls for a supersize rate hike soon, Williams said, "I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action."

articles.title_orig: Hospitals Rush to Patch Java Vulnerabilities
articles.title_zh: Hospitals Rush to Patch Java Vulnerabilities
articles.content_orig:
On November 17, 2026, details emerged exposing a critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in OpenJDK, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (dubbed "Java4Shell") with a CVSSv4.0 score of 9.2. The bug exists in the optimized assembly code handling AVX-512 Base64 decoding, allowing remote unauthenticated attackers to cause heap memory corruption. Triggering this flaw on affected systems can lead to remote code execution.
The "Java4Shell" vulnerability and exploit were discovered and disclosed by security firm Calif.
CVE-2026-114938 is a memory-corruption vulnerability residing in the optimized Base64 decoding intrinsic engine of the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). To maximize performance, OpenJDK uses an optimized implementation on supported x86-64 processors, based on AVX-512 VBMI instructions. However, the optimized assembly code miscalculates the output array bounds when handling inputs that contain an unexpected number of trailing padding characters (=).
When an input containing a specific sequence -such as 64 A characters followed by a single = - is parsed, the decoder's length calculation underflows to a negative value. This calculation mismatch causes an out-of-bounds write past the allocated heap memory buffer. Attackers can leverage this to overwrite adjacent object metadata, which can lead to code execution. We have proved that remote exploitation is feasible against standard Java applications such Jenkins, Confluence, and Apache Tomcat.
Like other memory safety issues, exploitation is possible with AI, but is not trivial. Our AI based vulnerability research harness, Wiz Atlas , managed to find and build a proof-of-concept exploit for this vulnerability within 2 hours, even before the full details were disclosed. Having said that, generalizing the exploit for an arbitrary target is difficult. We should expect adversaries to target commonplace Java applications, where specific builds and memory layouts repeat across targets. Motivated adversaries may tailor exploits with AI for specific targets, including home-grown applications.
Web Application Firewalls can help mitigate some of the exploits as they emerge in the wild. Since this vulnerability is rooted in OpenJDK itself, many possible code paths using user inputs may lead into the vulnerable code path, so it’s unlikely that WAF rules will be able to cover all possible paths, and will never be able to cover home grown applications completely. The best solution is upgrading to the latest OpenJDK version.
Prioritize externally facing, packaged Java applications, and make sure they are either patched or restricted from public access. Upgrade home-grown Java applications and update to the latest OpenJDK version containing the fix.
The vulnerability affects OpenJDK versions 17.0.6 and later, as well as downstream distributions, provided they run on x86-64 hardware supporting AVX-512 VBMI instruction sets (ARM64 processors are unaffected). Affected software distributions and hardware include:
OpenJDK Distributions: Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, and Oracle Java SE (specifically versions 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3).
Vulnerable CPU Architectures: Intel Xeon (Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids) and AMD EPYC/Ryzen (Zen 4 or newer).
Proven Vulnerable Applications (Pre-Auth RCE): Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, Keycloak, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and custom frameworks built on Spring Boot, Apache Struts, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, Netflix Spinnaker and Apache Tomcat.
Security teams should immediately prioritize the following mitigation steps:
Audit and Patch: Identify all systems running OpenJDK 17.0.6 or later on AVX-512-capable x86-64 hardware. Apply the official security patches released on November 17, 2026, or update to downstream vendor-supplied builds immediately.
Verify Hardware Vulnerability: Run the following command on Linux systems to check if your infrastructure is physically affected:
If all four CPU flags are present in the output, the host runs the vulnerable hardware execution path.
Implement JVM Runtime Workarounds: If immediate patching is not possible, apply one of the following flags to JVM startup parameters to completely neutralize the vulnerability. They may have performance impact on the application.
Disable Base64 Intrinsics (Recommended): -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics
Disable AVX-512 execution (x86-64 only): -XX:UseAVX=2
Isolate Internet-Facing Services: Temporarily restrict external network access to vulnerable management portals (e.g., Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak) until mitigations or updates are deployed.
Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.
On November 17, 2026 at 20:35 UTC, versions 1.26.1 & 1.26.2 of the Microsoft PyPI package agent-framework were published with an added credential stealer.  The package gets almost 200k downloads a month. The malicious versions have since been quarantined.
